title: Existentialism Is a Humanism
author: Jean-Paul Sartre
edition_analyzed: Commonly cited English translation by Carol Macomber, Yale University Press, 2007
target_audience: Individuals interested in modern European thought
People seeking an accessible introduction to Sartre’s ideas
core_themes: Ethics and moral responsibility without God
The possibility and meaning of humanism within existentialism
primary_purpose: To defend existentialism from common criticisms and clarify its meaning, arguing that existentialism is an optimistic humanism rooted in radical human freedom and moral responsibility in the absence of God.

structure_format.organization: Single extended lecture followed by Q&A (in some editions)
features: Examples from literature and everyday life

key_concepts_lessons: Existence precedes essence: humans define themselves through acts and choices, rather than conforming to pre-established natures.
Without God, humans bear full responsibility for their actions and values.
Freedom is absolute: we are “condemned to be free,” unable to shift responsibility onto fate, nature, or prescribed doctrines.
Anguish, forlornness, and despair are necessary consequences of freedom, but not excuses for inaction.
To choose for oneself is also to choose for all humanity—personal ethics have universal implications.
Existentialism does not lead to nihilism, quietism, or moral relativism, but affirms the possibility of authentic and engaged human life.
notable_features: Serves as the most popular introduction to Sartre’s philosophy
Addresses and rebuts contemporary criticisms from Marxists and Catholics
Popularizes existentialist language to a wider, non-academic audience
Introduces enduring existentialist slogans and ideas
cultural_historical_context: Delivered shortly after World War II in Paris, at a time when France was grappling with the legacy of collaboration, resistance, and reconstruction. Existentialism was gaining broad public attention and criticism. Sartre aimed to position existentialism as an ethical and optimistic philosophy for a secular, postwar world.
reception_impact: Became Sartre’s most accessible and widely read work
Credited with introducing existentialism to the general public
Generated controversy and debate among philosophers, clergy, and political thinkers
Criticized by some as oversimplifying existentialist philosophy
Remains a foundational text in twentieth-century philosophy and humanities education
comparable_titles: Being and Nothingness by Jean-Paul Sartre
Man's Search for Meaning by Viktor Frankl
The Myth of Sisyphus by Albert Camus
Fear and Trembling by Søren Kierkegaard
